Global Leveraged Finance Maturity Profile Supports Refinancing Flexibility

Near-term refinancing risk for leveraged finance issuers in the US and EMEA remains manageable, as most maturities originally due in 2026–2027 have been pushed out through extensions, repricings and refinancings, says Fitch Ratings. As a result, only a small share of leveraged loans (LLs) come due in 2026–2027.

LL maturities rise sharply to a steep wall starting in 2028. 34% of US and 40% of EMEA LLs mature in 2028-2029. High yield (HY) bonds, by contrast, have a more evenly spread maturity that peaks in 2029 in both regions, with roughly 20% maturing that year. These differing maturity profiles shape anchor refinancing volumes and affect pricing, market access and covenant flexibility — especially for lower-rated credits.

The US LL market has extended maturities on a year-over-year basis, with only 4% maturing within two years as of December 2025, compared to 6% a year ago. This push-out reflects robust activity, of which repricings, refinancings and recapitalisations represented 75%-85% of issuance across 2024-2025. Issuers used receptive markets to improve coupons, extend tenors and address near-term maturities, supporting financial flexibility into the late 2020s. By contrast, HY maturities show little year-over-year change, with 8%-9% of bonds maturing in 2026-2027.

EMEA HY near-term exposure fell to 15% from 26% a year earlier as issuers that previously deferred addressing legacy lowcoupon bonds refinanced into receptive 2025 markets. Fitch’s issuance data supports this finding, with 2025 EMEA HY issuance at the highest level since 2021, of which 70% represents recapitalizations and refinancings. With BB spreads compressing, many ‘BB’ issuers are waiting for the most favorable issuance windows to lock in the lowest possible rates. EMEA LL maturities are limited in 2026-2027 but concentrated in 2028, with around 21% (EUR80 billion) coming due that year.

Regional concentration creates a clear refinancing risk hotspot in EMEA. France accounts for the largest share of the 2028 maturity wall in both HY and LL — about 20% and 24%, respectively. French issuers also make up roughly 45% of Fitch’s European Top Tier and Tier 2 market concern loan list, and about 61% of that stressed/distressed cohort matures in 2028. This clustering increases sensitivity to market windows, pricing, and liquidity for French credits, potentially raising execution risk if volatility is elevated when refinancing needs peak. France’s prominence reflects the depth and sophistication of its LBO market, rather than a systemic country issue.

Credit quality composition remains a critical driver of refinancing flexibility. HY issuers tend to be larger and more diversified, with broader access to capital markets. BB-rated issuers account for 47% of the US HY universe and 55% of the EMEA HY universe. LLs are concentrated in lower-rating buckets: In the US LL market tracked by Fitch, 67% are rated ‘B’ and 14% are rated ‘CCC+’ or below. In EMEA, 85% are rated ‘B’ and 7% are rated ‘CCC+’ or below. Within the single ‘B’ cohort, ratings skew to the lower end of the category: about 30% of the maturity wall is rated ‘B-‘ in both regions.

Weaker-credit concentrations are especially high in the 2028-2029 maturity cohorts, and market access could bifurcate as refinancing windows narrow. In the US, issuers rated ‘B-‘ or below account for roughly 68% and 60% of 2028 and 2029 LL maturities; in EMEA, the shares are about 60% and 50%. Refinancing demand for ‘B-’ and lower credits has softened as capital has rotated toward higher-quality risk. This may limit access for ‘B-’ issuers, whose debt has traded at best near par and often at a discount.

Private-credit-led solutions and amend-and-extend deals may become more common, and some could potentially meet DDE criteria. For higher-quality HY issuers, a well-laddered maturity profile and a BB-heavy mix should support continued refinancing flexibility as the 2029 peak approaches.
